newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: "Go Go Go" Ramos urges, but students say "stop".
newsitem.headline: "Go Go Go" Ramos urges, but students say "stop".

text.p: President Fidel Ramos on Friday urged businessmen to "go, go, go" for the world's biggest free trade zone circling the Pacific, but Filipino student protesters cried "stop".

Ramos is enlisting the support of more than 400 chief executives from some of the region's biggest corporations to put into action promises by the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum to create a borderless economy embracing half the world's people by 2020.
In messages to the Asia-Pacific Business Forum and to APEC foreign and economic ministers at the start of a two-day meeting, Ramos said APEC's lofty goals must be backed by practical steps.
"Now we move into the action phase," he told the ministerial meeting that began to the stirring strains of "Land of Hope and Glory".
Outside the hall riot police scuffled with students demonstrating against APEC. The protesters waved banners saying "No to APEC" before being scattered by baton-wielding officers.

Hundreds of demonstrators have been marching in the Philippine capital to denounce APEC's pro-business vision of a single trading bloc for goods and services. They say it will benefit big business and rich nations at the expense of the poor.
They have promised more street action over the next two days leading to Monday's APEC summit in the former giant U.S. naval base at Subic Bay, 80 km (50 miles) from Manila.

Security was tight ahead of the summit. U.S. State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said Washington had received unspecified information about possible threats to American diplomats during the conference.
Burns told reporters the Philippines had taken steps to assure the security of American and other delegates but the United States felt compelled to alert the public to the danger.

The ministers approved an action plan for open trade to be endorsed by leaders of 18 APEC economies, including U.S. President Bill Clinton, Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto and Chinese President Jiang Zemin.
The so-called Manila Action Plan for APEC stitches together free-market initiatives proposed by individual members.

It will determine whether APEC remains a loosely-organised talking shop or evolves into a cohesive force in global trade and investment, setting the agenda in international forum such as the World Trade Organisation.
Ramos, who is transforming the Philippines from sick man of Asia to an emerging tiger economy, has staked much of his personal credibility on the document that will emerge from the summit.

"Let's go for it! Go Go Go!" he told business leaders, including the heads of corporations such as Salomon Inc of the United States, Japan's Itochu Corp and Southeast Asian phone giant Singapore Telecom.
In Indonesia last year, APEC set a timetable of 2010 for developed nations to completely open their markets and 2020 for developing economies.

The Manila meeting is intended to work out ways to achieve that aim and develop closer cooperation in a broad range of areas, including worker education, capital markets, infrastructure, technology and the environment.

"Now we must begin to take specific, concrete steps that will open up our economies and help lift the lives and living standards of our peoples," U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher told the ministers' meeting.
This year's summit coincides with a period of trouble for the Asian tigers whose economies have been hit by falling prices for their exports.
Sceptics say these economies, slowing after years of double-digit growth, are more likely to retreat behind barriers than expose themselves to further competition by tearing down obstacles to trade.

Nevertheless, in one sign of cooperation, support appeared to be coalescing around a U.S. plan to axe tariffs on the global trade in computers and related parts, including semiconductors, worth $1.8 trillion.

APEC groups Australia, Brunei, Canada, Chile, China, Hong Kong, Indonesia, Japan, Malaysia, Mexico, New Zealand, Papua New Guinea, the Philippines, Singapore, South Korea, Taiwan, Thailand and the United States.

APEC officials dashed hopes of countries such as Russia, India, Vietnam and Peru of speedy membership by saying no one else would be admitted until 1988 at the earliest when the APEC summit will be in Kuala Lumpur.
The 1997 summit will be in Vancouver.
